title: Revolutionizing procurement: Leveraging data and AI for ...
content:
### Quantitative estimates
- Done well, data can increase the pipeline of value creation initiatives by up to 200 percent.
- Sanofi:
  - Achieved an average 10 percent reduction in spend.
  - An advanced analytics platform reduced the time required to evaluate tenders by two-thirds.
  - Digitally enabled negotiations helped it increase the savings achieved by 281 percent.
- Teva Pharmaceuticals:
  - Achieved a more-than-tenfold improvement in supply resilience.
  - Smart spend category creation systems cut the time required to develop category strategies by 90 percent.
- Data infrastructure maturity:
  - 21 percent say their data infrastructure maturity is low.
  - Less than 70 percent of spend data stored in one place.
  - An additional 30 percent think they have average levels of data maturity.
- Best-in-class companies place 22 percent of procurement employees in analytics teams.
- A handful of data products can deliver 60 percent to 80 percent of the value at stake.
- Investments can be net positive in the eight-to-twelve-month range.
- A transformation typically takes six to eighteen months to make a step change.
- Many procurement organizations have road maps that aim to deploy fifteen or more data products every year.
- One WEF Lighthouse organization prioritized six use cases.
- That organization was able to double the value creation opportunities identified by the procurement function.

### Functions and use cases
| Area | Functions / use cases explicitly stated |
|---|---|
| Optimizing spend and demand | Spend categorization algorithms can create cleaned spend cubes seamlessly; demand forecasts and optimization; gen AI interfaces to interrogate spend, market, or specifications data; bots making trade decisions autonomously for standardized items with highly competitive markets such as transportations or temporary labor; automate contract generation; supply market analysis and strategy optimization; machine learning to analyze usage patterns and forecast demand to automatically generate sourcing scenarios and strategies based on inventory-level intelligence |
| Managing external drivers of profitability | Combine internal data with external market reports and databases; machine learning algorithms to uncover patterns and trends in commodity prices; real-time transparency on price volatility exposure; dynamically compute the should-cost of volatile commodities; negotiate with suppliers based on facts; assess impact of variation in input prices on product margins; analyze multiple scenarios to define actions to protect margins; recommend monthly the volume of palm oil derivatives to hedge for; optimize contracting strategy; adjust contract lengths and start dates; spot buy versus fixed price for a few months; redefine supplier regional footprint; obtain cost advantages through strategic agreements with selected Tier-N suppliers, including partial acquisition or vertical integration with value chain players obtaining disproportional margins |
| Managing supplier performance | Digital dashboards combining contract, invoice, and supplier delivery performance data; early warnings of performance deviations; steer operational interventions or supplier collaboration projects; parametric cleansheet tools calculating should-cost for thousands of items; optimize specifications; conduct robust, fact-based negotiations; automated tools producing smart intelligence on supplier risk profiles based on public data such as social media reports; automate creation of negotiation scripts, reports, emails, and contracts |
| Managing supply risks | Digital twin of supply chain; model all nodes across the globe; map material flows from tier-one suppliers in collaboration with suppliers; web data mining to close data gaps and build a picture of flows from across tier two to tier-n; near-live view of associated supply risk, cost, and carbon intensity; simulate risk level given forecasted business growth, occurrence of risk events, and effect of mitigation actions; assess implications of any type of change or disruption in highly complex and interconnected value chains; react to adverse events much earlier |
| Leading on sustainability | Estimate baseline for carbon emissions within the supply chain; evaluate upstream Scope 3 emissions; establish product-level emission reporting; share standards through existing procurement data infrastructure; integrate sustainability metrics with procurement data and advanced analytics; engage with, evaluate, and monitor sustainability progress of suppliers; reduce supply chain emissions by selecting products or suppliers that align with sustainability goals |

### Workflow closed-loop details
- Better data supports activities and decisions across the sourcing life cycle, from:
  - development of category strategies
  - assessment of potential suppliers
  - execution of negotiations
  - ongoing supplier performance management
- Parametric cleansheet tools automatically calculate should-cost for thousands of items, helping companies optimize specifications and conduct negotiations.
- Digital dashboards provide early warnings of performance deviations, which can steer operational interventions or supplier collaboration projects.
- The digital supply chain twin:
  - is built by combining collaboration with suppliers for tier-one material flows and web data mining for tier two to tier-n gaps
  - gives each node a near-live view of supply risk, cost, and carbon intensity
  - can simulate risk level based on forecasted business growth, risk events, and mitigation actions
  - allows procurement to assess implications of changes or disruptions and react much earlier
- Companies can use machine learning to analyze usage patterns and forecast demand to automatically generate sourcing scenarios and strategies based on inventory-level intelligence.
- Quick wins from the first use cases are critical in building momentum for the transformation.
- Transformation offices:
  - monitor progress versus the initial road map
  - track impact delivery rigorously
  - raise flags when solutions underdeliver
  - allow course correction
- One WEF Lighthouse:
  - tracks value creation and the number of users of each data product on a weekly basis
  - reviews with the CPO monthly
  - tracks and records the impact delivered on categories by each data product in the value tracking system
  - distinguishes which data products work and can be scaled versus which ones are stalling and require support
- One leading company interrupted development of a data product that required heavy manual work to compile product specifications data because the organization and technical architecture was not ready.
- Another company adapted its approach by bringing the business to the core of solution deployment after identifying low ownership of the value creation ideas.

### Adoption, ROI, and time-to-value
- The procurement function will act as a strategic lever for value protection and creation.
- Mastering data will empower procurement teams to achieve strategic objectives far beyond traditional cost, quality, and delivery metrics.
- Sanofi:
  - average 10 percent reduction in spend
  - time required to evaluate tenders reduced by two-thirds
  - savings achieved increased by 281 percent
- Teva Pharmaceuticals:
  - more-than-tenfold improvement in supply resilience
  - time required to develop category strategies cut by 90 percent
  - global procurement unit, based in Amsterdam, is the main contributor to its ambitious gross margin improvement program
- Data products can make investments net positive in the eight-to-twelve-month range.
- Turning procurement into a data-driven, AI-enabled organization typically takes six to eighteen months to make a step change.
- Low adoption can leave organizations stuck in pilot purgatory.
- Quick wins from first use cases help build momentum, foster excitement, and drive engagement across the organization.
- Focusing on adoption of AI technologies from day one helps procurement build solutions that work better, scale faster, and create more value for the organization.

### Required data
- Internal data:
  - spend
  - demand patterns
  - specifications
  - inventory-level intelligence
  - contract data
  - invoice data
  - supplier delivery performance data
- External data:
  - suppliers
  - market insights databases
  - wider web
  - external market reports and databases
  - public data such as social media reports
  - market insight databases
  - data from suppliers, customers, and the wider market
- Sustainability-related data:
  - expenditure-based data to estimate baseline carbon emissions within the supply chain
  - product-level emission reporting
  - consumption-based emission factors
  - existing procurement data infrastructure for sharing standards
- Supply chain twin data:
  - material flows from tier-one suppliers
  - web data mining to close data gaps
  - flows from tier two to tier-n
  - all nodes across the globe
  - sub-tier suppliers of raw materials
  - direct suppliers
  - internal manufacturing network
  - customers
  - logistic channels connecting these nodes

### KPIs
- Traditional metrics explicitly stated as not sufficient alone:
  - cost
  - quality
  - delivery
- KPIs and performance measures explicitly stated:
  - value creation initiatives pipeline
  - spend
  - demand forecast accuracy
  - share of spend exposed to a particular climate or geopolitical event
  - should-cost increase due to oil price fluctuations
  - alternative sources to a supplier in distress
  - price volatility exposure
  - product margins
  - monthly volume of palm oil derivatives to hedge for
  - supplier adherence to service-level agreements
  - should-cost for thousands of items
  - supplier risk profiles
  - supply risk
  - cost
  - carbon intensity
  - upstream Scope 3 emissions
  - supply chain emissions
  - value creation opportunities identified by the procurement function
  - number of users of each data product
  - impact delivered on categories by each data product
  - gross margin improvement program

### Risk and failure modes
- Price volatility
- Geopolitical tensions
- Sustainability imperatives
- High risks in supply market analysis
- Suppliers in distress
- Changes in input prices affecting product margins
- Supply chain disruptions
- Supply risks
- Carbon intensity concerns
- Pollution prevention concerns
- Unfair labor practices in the supply chain
- Issues with data quality and access
- Lack of clarity over the business case for new digital or AI applications
- Difficulty driving adoption of the new tools at scale
- Data infrastructure not ready to support the ambition
- Less than 70 percent of spend data stored in one place
- Single source of truth systems may still not have cleaned and categorized data
- Systems may lack important information from outside the procurement function, such as quality or specification data
- Systems may lack external data from suppliers, customers, and the wider market
- Technology-back approach: selecting software and solutions without a clear link to business value creation opportunities
- Pilot purgatory
- Quarterly results focus or short-term obligations preventing adoption
- Overly ambitious road maps aiming to deploy fifteen or more data products every year
- Capacity limitations to test, validate, industrialize, and scale a large volume of technical solutions
- IT function limitations in ability and capacity to steer and industrialize new tools
- New data products with unnecessary features that drive complexity and deteriorate user experience
- New data products not integrated seamlessly with existing procurement systems and processes
- Heavy manual work to compile product specifications data when organization and technical architecture was not ready
- Low ownership of value creation ideas by business partners
- Data governance processes remain a priority
- Procurement teams don’t typically have enough people skilled in data, analytics, and AI
description: Explore how AI and analytics are transforming procurement into a strategic function capable of driving significant business value, optimizing supply chains, and enhancing sustainability efforts.

title: Redefining procurement performance in the era of agentic AI
content:
### Quantitative estimates
| Item | Exact number(s) | Context |
|---|---:|---|
| Data use in procurement decision-making | less than 20 percent | “today’s procurement functions use less than 20 percent of the data available to them to support decision-making” |
| Contact center savings opportunities | 12 to 20 percent | Tech company use case for sourcing external services |
| Business process outsourcing and financial services spend savings opportunities | 20 to 29 percent | Tech company use case for sourcing external services |
| Procurement staff efficiency increase | 20 to 30 percent | Chemicals company autonomous sourcing in consumables category |
| Value capture increase | 1 to 3 percent | Chemicals company autonomous sourcing in consumables category |
| Analysis and emails time reduction | up to 90 percent | Telco player supporting price negotiations |
| Negotiation savings across vendors | 10 to 15 percent | Telco player supporting price negotiations |
| Leakage reduction | 4 percent | Pharmaceutical company invoice-to-contract compliance |
| Active inventory reduction | 30 percent | Aircraft OEM order execution and inventory levels based on production planning data |
| EBIT boost | around $700 million | Aircraft OEM order execution and inventory levels based on production planning data |
| Prototype to pilot | weeks | “go from prototype to pilot in weeks” |
| Pilot to scale | under a year | “from pilot to scale in under a year” |
| Procurement ROI definition | total value created divided by the total cost to achieve that impact | Explicit formula stated |

### Functions / use cases
| Organization / example | Functions / use cases | Specific AI agent actions |
|---|---|---|
| Tech company | Rebuild strategy for sourcing external services | One agent integrated spend and market data to generate real-time insights into price trends and savings opportunities; another simulated demand evolution under various market scenarios to hedge against volatility |
| Chemicals company | Autonomous sourcing in the consumables category | Agents automate tender preparation, identification and prequalification of suppliers, analysis of competing bids; another agent routes, tracks, and synthesizes queries and clarifications from suppliers during sourcing exercises |
| Telco player | Support price negotiations across long-tail spend on specialized software products | Agents prepare a comprehensive prenegotiation fact base; make real-time suggestions during negotiations; evaluate trade-offs between cost, service levels, and risk; automatically generate counteroffers to supplier proposals |
| Pharmaceutical company | Enforce invoice-to-contract compliance | Agents track supplier delivery performance and automatically check invoices and POs against contract terms |
| Aircraft OEM | Automate order execution and inventory levels based on production planning data | Agents automate order execution and inventory levels based on production planning data |
| General agentic AI examples | Category copilots; RFx generation and analytics; contract optimization; invoice-to-contract compliance; tail repricing systems | Listed as “no-regret agents” companies can apply off the shelf |

### Workflow closed-loop details
- AI agents “emulate human judgment, carry out multistep tasks, and continuously improve through learning loops.”
- AI agents “ingest complex datasets, reason through trade-offs, and autonomously generate options and recommendations.”
- Agentic AI can operate end to end:
  - identifying a strategic opportunity
  - sourcing suppliers
  - preparing commercial strategies
  - tracking performance post-award
- Procurement tasks will involve “teams of such agents, assembled to meet the requirements of each workflow and drawing on a diverse range of data sources.”
- AI’s true power is unlocked when applied across the full source-to-pay life cycle:
  - from early demand signals
  - to supplier performance tracking
  - integrated system allows compound benefits: faster decisions, lower costs, reduced risk
- “Establish feedback and learning loops.”
- “AI systems improve with use.”
- “Treat every cycle as a learning opportunity.”
- In the telco example:
  - agents prepare a prenegotiation fact base
  - make real-time suggestions during negotiations
  - evaluate trade-offs between cost, service levels, and risk
  - automatically generate counteroffers to supplier proposals
- In the chemicals example:
  - agents automate preparation of tenders
  - identification and prequalification of suppliers
  - analysis of competing bids
  - route, track, and synthesize queries and clarifications from suppliers during sourcing exercises
- In the pharmaceutical example:
  - agents track supplier delivery performance
  - automatically check invoices and POs against contract terms
- In the aircraft OEM example:
  - agents automate order execution
  - automate inventory levels based on production planning data

### Adoption / ROI / time-to-value
- “Leading companies that have embraced AI in procurement are already seeing outsized results.”
- “With the right foundation—typically a few key datasets and defined use cases—organizations can go from prototype to pilot in weeks, and from pilot to scale in under a year.”
- “This isn’t about massive ERP replacements or multiyear IT programs.”
- “It’s about targeted, high-ROI interventions that show results in months, not years.”
- “With the right sequencing, uplift is visible within months as agents move from pilot to production and the operating model evolves.”
- “AI in procurement is not a feature—it is a new foundation.”
- “The path is a recipe, not a pilot: Build the data spine; activate no-regret agents across sourcing, negotiation, and value preservation; and rewire roles and processes for human and agent ways of working.”

### Required data
| Requirement | Explicitly stated details |
|---|---|
| Key datasets | “typically a few key datasets” |
| Data accessibility | data must be “accessible” to AI agents |
| Data readiness | “Clean, connected data is the fuel of AI.” |
| Data spine | “common ‘data spine’ that provides a single source of truth across spend, suppliers, contracts, and market benchmarks” |
| Sources | “spend, suppliers, contracts, and market benchmarks” |
| Unstructured sources | agents may import data from “unstructured sources” |
| Diverse data sources | procurement tasks use agents “drawing on a diverse range of data sources” |
| Specific context and domain signals | “competitive edge comes from specific context and domain signals” |
| Data type examples | spend data, market data, market indices, production planning data, invoice and PO data, contract terms |

### KPIs / metrics / measures
- Procurement ROI:
  - “total value created divided by the total cost to achieve that impact”
  - Value includes:
    - realized savings
    - leakage avoided
    - working-capital and risk benefits
    - revenue enablement
  - Cost includes:
    - people (internal and external)
    - technology
    - data
    - change management
- “new KPIs” are needed as part of successful transformations.
- AI lifts value by:
  - expanding category management coverage beyond today’s bandwidth
  - improving outcomes in every negotiation
  - opening new pools of value such as automated tail-spend repricing
  - tighter compliance
- “faster decisions, lower costs, and reduced risk” are the integrated system outcomes.
- Procurement is positioned to shape broader enterprise outcomes:
  - resilience
  - sustainability
  - speed to market
  - innovation
  - growth
  - environmental, social, and governance (ESG)
  - supply-chain resilience
  - capital allocation

### Risk / failure modes
- Procurement teams are “struggling to keep pace.”
- Drivers of strain:
  - rapid shifts in the geopolitical environment
  - market dynamics
  - supply shocks
  - inflationary pressure
  - overwhelming volume of data
- Traditional operating models expose limits.
- Category teams are “buried under administrative workloads.”
- Sourcing cycles are “too slow.”
- Insight generation is “fragmented across siloed systems.”
- Growing gap between ambition and execution.
- Widening performance gap between digital leaders and laggards.
- Procurement functions use less than 20 percent of available data.
- Risks of fragmented, outdated, or incomplete data.
- Need to break down data siloes.
- Early AI use cases have been “narrow in scope.”
- Organizations face need for new capabilities:
  - prompt engineering
  - scenario evaluation
  - change management
- Executives must manage “embedding change, not just tools.”
- AI must be integrated into “the rhythms and rituals of how work gets done.”
- “Those who delay risk being left behind—not just by competitors, but by their own suppliers.”
description: Agentic AI is shifting the procurement function’s focus from transaction tasks to a strategic driver of growth, sustainability, and resilience.

| Enterprise setting | The AI chat assistant was deployed at a **Fortune 500 software firm**. |
| Functions / use cases | The generative AI tool provided **conversational guidance for customer support agents**.  
The chat assistant **read customer chats** and then **provided customer service agents with suggested responses**. |
| Workflow / closed-loop details | - The AI chat assistant **read customer chats**.  
- It then **provided customer service agents with suggested responses**.  
- **Agents were free to disregard the AI recommendation**.  
- **Agents remained responsible for the conversation**.  
- The AI recommendations were used by agents in the workflow; the researchers found that **agents who used the AI recommendations the most saw the largest increases in productivity**.  
- When the AI chat assistant was **not functioning**, agents were still **more productive than their pre-AI baseline**. |
| Quantitative estimates | - The AI tool increased the number of **successfully resolved customer issues by 14 percent**.  
- Newer and less experienced agents saw a **34 percent increase in the number of issues they were able to resolve per hour**.  
- The researchers found that the **quality of these agents’ conversations may have even decreased**.  
- The AI improved productivity through **a decrease in the time it took an agent to respond to a chat**, **an increase in the number of chats that an agent could respond to**, and **an increase in the share of successfully resolved conversations**. |
| Adoption / ROI / time-to-value | - The productivity gain was realized **mostly by the company’s newer, less experienced agents**.  
- The productivity increase for less experienced agents occurred because the generative AI **captured and emulated the characteristics of the most productive agents**.  
- **Longer tenured and more skilled workers saw little effect on their productivity**.  
- **On-the-job learning increased** when the AI chat assistant was used.  
- The article does **not explicitly state ROI, cost savings, implementation time, or payback period**. |
